Question: Which scenario is most important? Price engulfing an opposing FL/FTR or price engulfing both an opposing FL/FTR and the DP to EG?

Drawings below

The reason I ask: If engulfing is essentially clearing of orders, wouldn't engulfing the FL/FTR still leave significant orders at the Decision point to engulf just below? If IT's want to move price down, they need lots of buyers willing to acquire their short orders.... wouldn't there be lots of buyers at the DP to EG?

UJ - Chart with the decision points highlighted and labeled. I will keep building on this as more detail is added.

FL Box A:

A-1 DP to EG A-2 Buyers in control of price (FTR & FL) A-3 DP to break out of FL Box and make new high

FL Box B:

B-1- Decision to EG A-2 B-2 - Sellers in control of price (new FTR/FL) B-3 - DP to break out of Fl Box and make new low

I would say the B-1 engulfing A-2 is highly significant, and the FTR/FL that forms after the EG (B-2) should be seen as the main FL holding price down. There should be lots of sell orders at this level. Topside engulfs of B-2 would be significant as it would indicate bulls have taken over and there are more buy orders than sell orders in the market.

Close up of Fl Box B

Initially, I saw this as a fakeout. After thinking about order flow, I wonder why price came all the way up and formed a fakeout only to drop even further when the whole reason price retraced after the engulf of FL Box A by FL Box B was to gather orders at the origin of the engulf. Why do this twice? Am I mis understanding what is happening in the red circle? Is this a fakeout to true supply or is this something else?

I should also add an important engulf and RT I missed previously. When price breaks in to the top of the red rectangle containing FL Box A, it engulfs A-3. This engulf and RT forms the first FL Box of price as it works its way through FL Box A.

This may be important when it comes to understanding Salivan's entry. The dark green rectangle shows where another engulf and deep RT occurs. This is the last engulf before the main engulf that takes out the lower extreme limit of FL Box A.

Notice how close Salivan's entry comes to the bottom of the dark green rectangle.....

Hi H,

I think what I came up with yesterday was pure crap. I tried applying it since that great moment of discovery to no avail. I think those decisions I pointed out to are nothing more than an indication that we've broken back into the main important zone which is the original FL. I think it was pure chance that it looked so good on the chart yesterday...

Now what Mr. IF says over and over is to look for areas where tricks were played in the past. Such areas for me come at a previous swing high/low that may have been broken down then up then down then up for a final move down suppose. The reason I am getting into this is because if we have the sequence of flag limits wrong then everything else will be wrong.

What I've taken in so far about flag limits is the following: ( I might be completely wrong) 1- The most important FLs are those that are created after engulfing an opposite FL. 2- The last FL in a rally (b4 RBD is established) is the most important one... the last FL in a drop (b4 DBR is established) is the most important one. 3- The first FL coming out of a new zone i.e. RBD/DBR that takes out another opposite FL (2-) or an important swing high/low (that gave the lowest low/highest high) has great value.

4- Sometime FL cannot be well seen defined as per breaking an important SR or another opposite FL, but often we can tell of their existence by looking at where price held several times in a row. 5- Flipped FLs are important as they may at times of non visibility of the new ones define the new zone for us. 6- The best trades to be taken are the FTBs to FLs. 7- Price will often FO in the zone between the the first FL that come out of a RBD/DBR and the RBD/DBR itself. 8- A FL may have other FLs inside it, an important one would be an opposite one that got faked out, then flipped. 9- The decision to break out of an FL is often tradable. 10- A FL is a RBR/DBD and often defined as one candle - the whole range of that candle.

I will also add what seniors say here often and that is FL indicate the end of momentum.

Good points, Lucien. It is definitely making me think harder...

Salivan and IF both are confident in the trades they take...they have tight stops with large limits. They trade in the direction of an engulf that hasn't hit its target. Trading with such tight stops requires knowing exactly where the last extreme set of orders/liquidity lies within a FL. You are right to say that we should look for trades in areas where tricks were played in the past. In every one of Salivan's trades there is a fakeout that recently occurred and his entries occur near these fakeouts.

An analogy I think of: The fakeout is like a tornado that destroys a town and everyone in it. There is nothing good left for the survivors so most people pack up and leave town looking for a new place to live. A few people end up going back to this town a few days later in a last ditch effort to grab any money/gold/valuables left behind. Everyone left in such a hurry that inevitably there were some valuables left behind.These people gather up all the valuables they can find and hop on the last train leaving town. Salivan is always one of the people who go back to grab whatever valuables they can find

If the point of a fakeout is to grab liquidity by trapping traders into taking the wrong position and/or triggering stop loss orders, it would make sense that a fakeout would happen in an extreme area of a FL - the extreme opposite of the engulf and target. If this is true, we can conclude that fakeouts occur in an extreme part of a flag. If a fakeout takes all liquidity in its path, it would logically make sense that no orders would be left in the area where the fakeout occurred.

We know fakeouts tend to spike in to areas of liquidity - which is usually an extreme part of a FL or FTR. Maybe the goal is to look for the last place where orders exist after the fakeout has cleared out the extreme set of orders in the flag it broke in to. I would say the last fresh set of orders would be found in the extreme portion of the FL that forms after the first engulf of the base/decision to fakeout. The FL/FTR that forms after the engulf of the DP to FO would be the last place for price to return to and get orders before continuing on to its target.

As opportunists who want to gather up value easily, we start looking around for other towns where tornadoes have recently destroyed everything. We wait for everyone to start migrating out of the town looking for a better place to live and that's when we show up to grab what is left. This is what we should be doing in these charts - looking for places where tornadoes have touched down but nobody has come back yet.

Not sure if this is right though...

Analogy applied to one of salivan's trades on AUD-USD:

Please refer to chart below:

The origin of the initial move down began at the RBD F/O labeled "1". When price moves back up and engulfs the extreme topside of Fl 1 it creates a new high, which allows us to draw a FL Box around the entire move. (See the dotted black rectangle). Since the origin of the initial move down has been engulfed to the upside (labeled as EG "A"), we can be confident the market is moving up. We should anticipate Price deeply RT to the last set of orders within the FL Box. We want to only get in at the edge of a PAZ.

Salivan took the trade at the extreme bottom of the HTF FL Box (dotted rectangle) but he also looked for S/R flip zones as well on the lower time frames.This is very similar to #8 in Lucien's post (post #783 for reference).

He wrote: 8- A FL may have other FLs inside it, an important one would be an opposite one that got faked out, then flipped.

This would explain Salivan's confidence in taking a trade - there is no reason for another F/O to occur below his entry because there are no more orders left.
